title: The 6% excise tax (over-contribute by $1,000)

concepts.title: The over-contribution mechanic
concepts.body: Contributing more than the 2026 limit ($7,500, or $8,600 at 50+) to a Roth IRA is an excess contribution. The IRS penalty for an excess contribution is a 6% excise tax — applied every year the excess remains in the account. The 6% is on the excess amount, not on the total balance.

concepts.title: The $1,000 example
concepts.body: Say you over-contribute by $1,000 — contributed $8,500 instead of $7,500. The 6% excise tax is $1,000 × 0.06 = $60 per year. If you leave the excess in for 5 years, that's $300 in excise tax. Plus the $1,000 of excess is still in the account — and earnings on it are subject to a second 6% tax until corrected.

concepts.title: The fix: recharacterize or withdraw the excess (with earnings)
concepts.body: Two paths. Path one: recharacterize the excess as a traditional IRA contribution (if you're eligible). Path two: withdraw the excess plus attributable earnings before your tax filing deadline (including extensions). File Form 5329 to report and pay the 6% — or to claim the withdrawal exception. Correct the mistake; the 6% stops.

sources: IRS — IRC §4973 — Excise tax on excess contributions to certain tax-favored accounts
IRS Form 5329 — Additional Taxes on Qualified Plans (including Section 4973)
IRS Pub 590-A — Excess Roth IRA contributions
